name: Silymarin (milk thistle)

lead: Silymarin is the active extract of milk thistle, mainly sold as a liver-support supplement. People who take it for looks hope its antioxidant activity gives clearer, healthier-looking skin and slower visible ageing.

It is described as scavenging free radicals and chelating metals, with anti-inflammatory effects, and proposed skin benefits include protection from UV damage and inflammation. No human trials for skin or cosmetic outcomes were found.

paras: It is taken as a standardised capsule or tablet supplement, usually daily and over a long period. People pair it with ordinary skincare and sun protection rather than using it alone.
It may inhibit drug-metabolising enzymes and transporters, so interactions with medicines cannot be excluded; pregnancy data are limited.

angle.text: Silymarin is a milk thistle liver supplement that some people take for its antioxidant chemistry, hoping for clearer skin or slower visible ageing. The skin role is proposed; no human skin trials were found.

lead: Silymarin is a standardised extract of milk thistle (Silybum marianum) containing flavonolignans, chiefly silibinin (silybin), along with silychristin and silidianin.[1] It is used mainly as a liver-support supplement and has been studied for antioxidant activity.[2][3]

Its link to appearance comes through proposed skin effects. Wikipedia notes proposed skin benefits such as protection from UV damage and inflammation, but reports no human clinical trials for skin or cosmetic use.[1]
infobox: Oral supplement; IV silibinin in Europe for Amanita poisoning[1]

paras: Intravenous silibinin is approved in Europe for Amanita mushroom poisoning, some EU countries approve oral silymarin as adjunct therapy in chronic hepatitis and cirrhosis, and elsewhere it is sold as a dietary supplement.[1]

Evidence for chronic liver disease is described as limited and mixed; a meta-analysis found no effect on all-cause mortality in cirrhosis.[1] Reviews discuss liver applications and antioxidant mechanisms.[2][3][4]
Silymarin may inhibit P-glycoprotein and cytochrome P450 enzymes, so interactions with some drugs cannot be excluded; pregnancy data are limited.[1]

No studies found of silymarin for appearance outcomes. Clinical research concerns other conditions, including liver disease,[3][4] and registered trials in trichotillomania (NCT02473913) and body dysmorphic disorder (NCT02843451, withdrawn).[5][6]
